# Prices, supply and demand (`price_mechanism_supply_demand`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/economy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Economy & finance (`economy`)
- Deps: helped by coinage, division_of_labour
- Core idea: Where people may buy and sell freely, the price rises when a good is scarce relative to buyers and falls when it is plentiful. A high price does two jobs at once: it rations what there is among buyers willing and able to pay, and it draws in more supply, as merchants bring grain from where it is cheap and farmers sow more. A price fixed below the market level empties the shops and stops supply; one fixed above it leaves goods unsold. In a famine the best help is to give the poor money or work so they can buy, and let the high price pull grain in, while the state buys and moves grain itself if traders cannot.
- Pitfalls:
  - Capping prices in a dearth: grain vanishes from the market and suppliers stop coming (Diocletian's edict 301, the French maximum 1793)
  - Blaming merchants for a scarcity or for a rise caused by debasement, and so driving away the trade that would end it
  - Assuming famines come only from lack of food: many came from collapsing wages or prices of what the poor sell (Sen)
  - Believing markets always work: monopoly, collusion, cornering and fraud need rules and inspection
  - Preaching a 'just price' fixed by custom while costs change
- History: mesopotamia: c. 1800 BC – the laws of Eshnunna open with a list of fixed prices, an early attempt to set prices by law; china: c. 4th–1st c. BC – the Guanzi 'light and heavy' chapters analyse how scarcity moves prices and how the state can trade to steady them; c. 90 BC Sima Qian (Shiji ch. 129) argues that high prices draw goods in and low ones send them away; rome: 301 – Diocletian's Edict on Maximum Prices, widely ignored and abandoned; islamic: 7th c. – a hadith has the Prophet refusing to fix prices; 13th–14th c. Ibn Taymiyya distinguishes unjust price fixing from intervention to secure a fair price when sellers exploit necessity; 1377 Ibn Khaldun on prices, demand and urban wealth; europe: 16th c. – Salamanca theologians on prices and money; 1776 Adam Smith; 1838 Cournot's demand function; 1890 Marshall's supply and demand curves
- Read:
  - Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations (1776)
  - Alfred Marshall, Principles of Economics (1890)
  - Amartya Sen, Poverty and Famines: An Essay on Entitlement and Deprivation (1981)
